title: Power Beats Wealth and Fame Combined in AI Fantasy Prompts
summary: Power fantasies appeared in prompts from 449 Magic Hour creators, 91% more than the 235 creators depicting wealth or fame.
body_markdown:
## Quick answer


**Power fantasies appeared in prompts from 449 observed Magic Hour creators, 91% more than the 235 creators who depicted becoming rich or famous.**


The comparison uses distinct creators and deduplicates people appearing in both wealth and fame categories.


Power fantasies appeared in prompts from 449 observed Magic Hour creators, 91% more than the 235 creators who depicted becoming rich or famous.


The comparison uses explicit transformation or aspiration language. The power category includes becoming powerful, a leader, a boss or a CEO. The wealth and fame comparison includes becoming rich, wealthy, a millionaire, a billionaire, famous, a celebrity or a superstar. Creators appearing in both wealth and fame were counted once.


The finding describes stories made by Magic Hour creators. It does not reveal creators’ personal ambitions, establish why they chose a theme or represent the general public.


## Power wins across every medium


Power language appeared for 349 video creators, compared with 162 using wealth or fame language. In audio, the comparison was 67 versus 42. In images, it was 38 versus 35.


The strongest component was direct powerful language, used by 394 creators. Leader appeared for 36, boss for 18 and CEO for nine. Categories can overlap.


## What the finding means


AI fantasy prompts frequently frame aspiration as influence, authority or transformation rather than money or celebrity alone. That is an observed storytelling pattern, not evidence that Magic Hour creators personally value power over wealth or fame.


## Methodology


The analysis covers completed, enabled, nondeleted Magic Hour image, video and audio projects from June 16, 2023 through September 19, 2026. It counts distinct observed creators whose stored prompt text paired aspiration or transformation language with documented power, wealth or fame expressions.


Templates, logged automated free-tool tasks, blank prompts, exact prompts reused by five or more creators in the same month, adult content, named political and celebrity subjects, and prominent copyrighted-character contexts were excluded. Wealth and fame were deduplicated at the creator level. Results were checked across media, workflows, time periods, direct component terms and heavy-user concentration.


The 2x estimate for unlogged free-tool usage is not included in observed counts or percentages. Magic Hour users are not representative of everyone, and the findings should not be generalized to the public.


No raw prompts, personal information, project identifiers or user media are published.
